clue.text: The value of a linguistic element for poet

parts.note: a word is a linguistic element; with the possessive from 'of a' it gives word's
worth means value

explanation.surface: A question about how much a single word is worth to someone who writes verse.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the clue as a phrase: 'the value of a linguistic element' is a word's worth, run together as one name.
explanation.definitionFit: William Wordsworth was the English Romantic poet of the Lake District.

clue.text: Light material, twisted cotton

explanation.surface: Describing the stuff a candle is made from: a twist of cotton thread.
explanation.definitionFit: The burning strand of a candle or lamp is a length of twisted cotton thread, so both senses name that thread.

clue.text: Heard again what spider did in cave

explanation.surface: A court case and the legend of the spider in the cave set side by side.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert the Bruce, hiding in a cave, watched a spider fail and try again until it spun its web; it tried once more. A case heard a second time in court is also this.
explanation.definitionFit: A case re-heard by a court has been tried a second time, and the persistent spider in the Bruce legend kept trying again.

clue.text: found in barnacle

parts.note: the middle of the word barnacle spells N-A-C-L, the chemical formula NaCl of common salt, so the clue points at the compound sitting inside the word

explanation.surface: A note about something living inside a barnacle shell.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole clue: barNACLe holds NaCl, the chemical formula of common salt, so what is 'found in barnacle' is that compound spelt out in full.
explanation.definitionFit: NaCl is the formula of common table salt, the compound written out here by its chemical name.

clue.text: Business types whose needs are well satisfied?

definitions.text: Business types whose needs are well satisfied?

parts.words: Business types whose needs are well satisfied?
parts.note: the needs of these business people are met by wells in the oil-drilling sense, not in the sense of being done well

explanation.surface: Executives whose requirements are thoroughly met.
explanation.walkthrough: 'well satisfied' reads as 'fully satisfied', but the well is an oil well that supplies what these traders need.
explanation.definitionFit: Petroleum executives depend on drilled wells for the crude they sell.

clue.text: Provided with a new body image

definitions.text: Provided with a new body image

parts.words: Provided with a new body image
parts.note: body image usually means how one sees one's own figure, but here it is a literal picture inked onto the skin

explanation.surface: Someone given a fresh perception of their own physique.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Body image' is a phrase from psychology; here it is an actual image put on the body by a needle and ink.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who has had ink pictures put permanently into their skin has a new picture on their body.

clue.text: A territory in the East that appears endless?

definitions.text: A territory in the East that appears endless?

parts.words: A territory in the East that appears endless?
parts.note: the eastern continent is vast enough to seem to go on forever, and its name begins and ends with the same letter, so it loops round with no visible end

explanation.surface: A vast eastern land stretching beyond the horizon.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the second reading: the name starts and finishes with A, so written in a ring it seems to have no end.
explanation.definitionFit: The largest continent lies in the East and covers an immense expanse of land.

clue.text: What appears on shore, making one run outside hotel

indicators.note: outside says the first piece is wrapped round the second

parts.note: in cricket a single is one run
H is Hotel in the radio alphabet

explanation.surface: Something seen on the beach, involving a lone jogger passing a hotel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outside' puts SINGLE around H. A single is a one-run score in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: Shingle is the mass of small pebbles that covers many British beaches.

clue.text: Get everyone to repeat what Bellman's crew did

parts.note: all means everyone
to iterate is to repeat

explanation.surface: An instruction to make the whole crew echo what was said.
explanation.walkthrough: In Lewis Carroll's The Hunting of the Snark the Bellman's crew are the Boots, Baker, Banker, Barrister and so on: every name starts with B.
explanation.definitionFit: Carroll's crew members all have names starting with the same letter, the defining trait of repeated initial sounds.

clue.text: Fault gifts I'd packed for deputy leaders

parts.note: a vice is a moral fault

indicators.note: packed says one piece is stuffed inside the other

parts.note: presents are gifts
I'd contracted to its letters gives ID

explanation.surface: A complaint about presents stuffed with something for the second-in-command.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fault' looks like a verb accusing the gifts, but it is a noun; 'packed' signals the container.
explanation.definitionFit: A vice-president is a deputy who stands in for the head of an organisation or state.

clue.text: Strange dialect featured in Cronin novel

indicators.note: strange suggests the following word is turned into something odd, its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: An odd regional way of speaking that appears in a book by A J Cronin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strange' rearranges DIALECT. A J Cronin's 1937 novel is The Citadel, about a doctor in Welsh mining towns.
explanation.definitionFit: The Citadel is the title of A J Cronin's best-known novel about medicine.

clue.text: In experiment, I see it's possessing little weight

indicators.note: In placed before the pieces says they go inside the following word

parts.note: a trial is an experiment
V stands for vide, Latin for see, used in references

explanation.surface: A scientist observes something lightweight during a test.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' puts I and V inside TRIAL. V is the abbreviation of vide, 'see', in footnotes.
explanation.definitionFit: Something of little weight is unimportant, of no real consequence.

clue.text: Performances by skaters — or people in crew?

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a set of displays on ice might really be about a rowing team.
explanation.walkthrough: A rowing eight has eight oarsmen, so each is one of the figures, or persons, of the eight.
explanation.definitionFit: Skaters trace looping double-circle patterns on the ice, and the persons in a rowing eight are its members.

clue.text: Play I abandoned was flourishing

parts.note: Brand is a verse play by Henrik Ibsen
shed means cast off or abandoned

explanation.surface: A dramatist gives up a script that had been doing well.
explanation.walkthrough: Brand is Ibsen's 1865 verse drama; 'Play' here is that title, not a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To brandish a sword is to wave it about showily, and waving a weapon is flourishing it.

clue.text: Edit bloody part for play

parts.note: blood is red, so bloody suggests red
an act is a part of a stage play

explanation.surface: A director cutting the gory section from a stage show.
explanation.definitionFit: To redact a document is to edit it, often by blacking out sensitive words.

clue.text: Try, try again? I agree with that!

parts.note: a judge hears a case when trying it
the second try is another hearing

explanation.surface: Someone backing the old motto about persevering after failure.
explanation.walkthrough: To try a case in court is to hear it, so 'try, try' gives the word twice; 'again' only joins.
explanation.definitionFit: The cry is shouted in Parliament and meetings to show approval of what a speaker has said.

clue.text: Time in a margin of victory shown fully

indicators.note: in says the first piece goes inside the others

parts.note: in horse racing a winner may win by a length

explanation.surface: A race result showing how long a winner won by.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts T inside A LENGTH, between the A and the LENGTH.
explanation.definitionFit: To discuss something in great detail and for a long while is to treat it thoroughly.

clue.text: Fine character of group of people, by no means common

definitions.text: group of people, by no means common

explanation.surface: Praise for a fine-spirited set of people who are far from ordinary.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain 'commoners' are those without title, so a group by no means common is the peerage.
explanation.definitionFit: Nobility is moral excellence of character, and also the aristocratic class of titled peers.

clue.text: Special action taken with book about plants

indicators.note: special suggests a reworked form, so the letters of the next word are rearranged

explanation.surface: A special move involving a book on gardening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Special' reads as an adjective on action, but it is the anagram signal; 'taken with' only joins.
explanation.definitionFit: Botanic means relating to botany, the study of plant life.

clue.text: Defensive unit wants score to change before extra time

indicators.note: before puts the rearranged letters ahead of the extra letter
the word score has to change, its letters set in a new order

parts.note: T stands for time

explanation.surface: A football team's defence needs the scoreline to alter before the match goes into extra time.
explanation.walkthrough: The football surface makes 'Defensive unit' look like a back line, but it is a guard travelling alongside; 'to change' signals the anagram and 'before' the order.
explanation.definitionFit: An escort is a guard of ships or troops travelling alongside to protect something.

clue.text: Admit to aim that helps the opposition

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase for a noun: a thing that helps the other team

parts.note: to own up to, or own, means to admit
a goal is an aim

explanation.surface: Confessing to an ambition that ends up helping one's rivals.
explanation.definitionFit: Scoring into your own net in football gives the opposing side a point.

clue.text: Little boys like Basil

parts.note: Herb is a short form of the boy's name Herbert
Al is a short form of the boy's name Albert

explanation.surface: Young lads who are fond of someone called Basil.
explanation.walkthrough: Basil looks like a man's name to go with the boys, but it is the kitchen plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Basil is a culinary plant, so something resembling it is of that plant kind.

clue.text: "Mutually reliant" — expression used mainly in this publication

indicators.note: in says the shortened word goes inside the paper's name

parts.note: the puzzle appeared in The Independent newspaper

indicators.note: mainly means most of the word, its final letter cut off

parts.note: a term is an expression

explanation.surface: A phrase that crops up often in this very paper.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is in quotation marks; 'this publication' is the newspaper the puzzle ran in, and 'mainly' cuts the last letter of the expression.
explanation.definitionFit: Things or people that rely on each other each depend on the other.

clue.text: Essay about love in the city of Paris

indicators.note: about says the first word goes round the second

parts.note: to essay is to try
love is zero in tennis, giving O

explanation.surface: A piece of writing on romance in the French capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts O inside TRY. Paris is the Trojan prince of Greek myth, not the French capital.
explanation.definitionFit: Paris, son of Priam, was a prince of the ancient city besieged by the Greeks.

clue.text: Shamefaced boxer, say, after suspension

indicators.note: after puts the dog behind the suspension

parts.note: hanging is suspension
a boxer is a breed of dog

explanation.surface: A boxer looking sheepish after being suspended from fighting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boxer' suggests a fighter suspended from the ring, but it is the dog breed; 'say' marks it as an example and 'after' gives the order.
explanation.definitionFit: A hangdog look is guilty and abashed, like a dog that knows it misbehaved.

clue.text: European's greeting some club on journey

indicators.note: some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A golfer's travelling companion greets someone from the Continent.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the French for good day, the standard hello in France.

clue.text: Cotton fabric no cricketer wants to get

explanation.surface: Describing a cloth that batters dread being associated with.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a duck is a score of nothing, the batsman out without a run.
explanation.definitionFit: Duck is a heavy plain-woven cotton cloth, and a batsman out for zero has made a nought.

clue.text: A piece of cake for Peter Pan?

explanation.surface: Asking whether J M Barrie's story about the boy who never grew up was easy.
explanation.walkthrough: Peter Pan is a play written for children, and 'a piece of cake' means something easy.
explanation.definitionFit: Something very easy is no trouble at all, and Barrie's drama is a stage piece aimed at young audiences.
